extracted.intended_audience: scientists, naturalists, philosophers, and the educated public interested in evolution and ethics (late 19th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging scientific theories (especially evolutionary theory) and for assessing moral claims under a naturalistic/scientific ethics. Covers evidence standards, methodological principles, and moral-evaluative norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: The essence of the scientific spirit is criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: "The essence of the scientific spirit is criticism. It tells us that, to whatever doctrine claiming our assent, we should reply, Take it if you can compel it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate theories by subjecting them to critical scrutiny and attempt to refute them; prefer an attitude that only accepts doctrines that can withstand sustained critical challenge. Anti-pattern: uncritical acceptance or submission to authority or fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: A theory's right to exist is its resistance to rivals
rubrics_metrics.description: "A theory is a species of thinking, and its right to exist is coextensive with its power of resisting extinction by its rivals."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a theory's plausibility by its explanatory power relative to alternative hypotheses and its durability under competing explanations. Emphasize comparative, competitive testing rather than rhetorical or sentimental appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary/direct evidence for evolution must come from paleontology
rubrics_metrics.description: "Primary and direct evidence in favor of evolution can be furnished only by paleontology. The geological record, so soon as it approaches completeness, must, when properly questioned, yield either an affirmative or a negative answer."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require fossil record evidence showing the expected marks of descent-with-modification (gradations, transitional forms). Use the geological sequence as a decisive empirical test when sufficiently complete; absence of evidence may reflect incompleteness of record rather than refutation, but completeness should decide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformitarianism as a methodological standard
rubrics_metrics.description: "The progress of scientific geology has elevated the fundamental principle of uniformitarianism, that the explanation of the past is to be sought in the study of the present, into the position of an axiom."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor explanations that invoke known present-day natural causes and processes rather than extraordinary, ad hoc catastrophes. Apply the same natural causal principles across past and present when evaluating historical theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of gradation/transitional links
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is an obvious consequence ... that all plants and animals ... must, at one time or other, have been connected by direct or indirect intermediate gradations..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A genuine evolutionary account should predict intermediates/connectivity between groups; seek and value transitional fossils and anatomical/developmental intermediates (e.g., Archaeopteryx, toothed birds) as confirmatory evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embryological similarity as evidence for common descent
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first beginnings of all the higher forms of animal life are similar ... the process of development ... is a true process of evolution — a progress from almost formless to more or less highly organized matter."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative embryology (similar early stages, common developmental processes) to test hypotheses of relationship and descent; concordance between embryology and other lines of evidence strengthens evolutionary explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and improvement of the fossil record affects hypothesis status
rubrics_metrics.description: Huxley's account: discoveries since 1859 (e.g., Pikermi fossils, Western American tertiaries) have increased known fossils 'fifty-fold' and moved some propositions from hypothesis to demonstrable fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to revise the confidence in a theory as the empirical base grows; newly discovered fossils or data can turn previously speculative claims into well-supported conclusions. Anti-pattern: clinging to a verdict despite substantial new evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate beliefs by both psychological receptivity and logical cogency of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: "Every belief is the product of two factors: the first is the state of the mind to which the evidence in favor of that belief is presented; and the second is the logical cogency of the evidence itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing acceptance of a doctrine, consider both (a) the audience's prior knowledge, biases, and readiness to receive evidence, and (b) the intrinsic strength and logic of the evidence. Distinguish sociological explanations for belief from purely epistemic justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral judgments most emphatically apply to actions affecting others
rubrics_metrics.description: "The words good and bad are most emphatically applied to those deeds by which men affect one another ... we pronounce our most emphatic judgments upon those acts by which men affect one another, because in them we see most conspicuously the conflict of higher and lower impulses."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In ethical assessment, prioritize social consequences and actions that impact other persons; such acts reveal conflicts of impulses and thus demand strongest moral scrutiny. Private or purely individual acts may be morally relevant but often less central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish praise-worthy moral excellence from enforceable duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Huxley: acts we praise highly (patriotism, public spirit) differ from acts commonly 'enforced' (fulfillment of contract, ordinary civic duties); public opinion and legal enforcement operate on different classes of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating moral systems or policies, separate (a) actions that deserve social approbation and reinforcement because they advance higher goods, from (b) baseline duties that are subject to enforcement. Recognize that praise reinforces higher motives while enforcement secures ordinary cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentionality matters because of differential societal consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Responding to the murder/accident objection: although judged by consequences, intention matters because willful offenders do not suffer the consequences and thus place the burden on society (e.g., punishment, prevention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In moral evaluation, account for the agent's intent since intent affects future risk, social deterrence, and allocation of burdens; differentiate between careless acts and malicious acts in both judgment and sanctioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a 'perfect action' by its consequences tending to life/happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: "A perfect action is one all the consequences and relations of which are satisfactory, as tending to happiness or life; and, therefore, no action which has any accompaniment of pain ... can be a perfect action."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under a consequentialist/naturalistic ethic, evaluate actions by the totality of consequences for preservation and improvement of life and happiness. Recognize that painful means or accompanying suffering may render actions imperfect even when motives are pure; practical decision-making often requires choosing among imperfect options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use guarded ethical language to avoid misleading implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of Spencer's phrase that actions with any painful concomitant are 'partially wrong'—Huxley suggests more guarded formulations to avoid 'crooked casuistry of the heart.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate ethical claims with care to avoid linguistic overreach that misleads or invites perverse casuistry; prefer precise qualifications (e.g., 'imperfect action' vs 'partially wrong') when addressing complex moral trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social approval functions as a mechanism to reinforce moral evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: "This social approval must powerfully reenforce the motives which prompt to such actions, but which, without social support, might not have vigor enough to fully assert themselves against countervailing motives."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In designing or evaluating moral systems, acknowledge the normative role of praise, honor, and public esteem as tools to strengthen higher motives and sustain altruistic behaviors. Consider how cultural institutions and public sentiments contribute to moral development.
